One hospice called at two weeks after the death and the other at six weeks; both offered a support group and individual support. Of 388 relatives called at two weeks, 21 percent accepted support, compared with 34 percent of 402 relatives called at six weeks. Relatives called at two weeks more often said they were still busy with practical matters and asked to be called later. Acceptance was lower among men at both sites. The hospices differed in size and staffing, so the comparison may be confounded by site."},{"title":"Proactive telephone outreach compared with a written invitation for bereavement support after expected deaths: a controlled before-after study","authors":"Oduya-Castellanos R, Brandt-Mensah L","year":2019,"venue":"Palliative Services Review","doi":"10.5555/psr.2019.0447","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"A community palliative care service replaced its written invitation to bereavement support with a proactive telephone call by a trained volunteer, while a neighbouring service kept the letter. Over 12 months before and 12 months after the change, uptake of any bereavement support rose from 18 percent to 37 percent in the intervention service and was unchanged at 16 percent in the comparison service. Most of the additional uptake was for one-to-one support rather than groups. Volunteers reported that calls lasted a median of 11 minutes. Families were not asked about their experience of the call, and the two services served different populations."},{"title":"Bereavement risk screening at the time of death and targeted follow-up: uptake by assessed risk level in a regional palliative care network","authors":"Nakashima-Holt E, Adeyemi-Varga S, Petit-Lorenz K","year":2021,"venue":"Grief and Palliative Practice","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Five palliative care services in one region introduced a brief bereavement risk screen completed by the nurse at the time of death. Relatives rated high risk were offered a proactive call from a social worker, and other relatives were sent a letter. Among 1,146 screened relatives, 19 percent were rated high risk. Uptake of support was 52 percent among high-risk relatives and 13 percent among the others. Screening was completed for 71 percent of deaths and less often for deaths at night. The study did not assess whether the risk screen predicted later prolonged grief, and relatives rated low risk who later asked for help were not counted."},{"title":"Who takes up hospice bereavement support? Differences by sex, language and distance in five years of service records","authors":"Whitfield-Achebe D, Szabo-Moreau I","year":2018,"venue":"Journal of Hospice Family Care","doi":"10.5555/jhfc.2018.0088","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We examined five years of bereavement service records at one hospice, covering 2,034 relatives who were offered support. Overall uptake was 22 percent. Uptake was 14 percent among men and 27 percent among women, 9 percent among relatives who needed an interpreter, and 12 percent among relatives living more than 50 kilometres from the hospice. Relatives of patients who died at home took up support less often than relatives of patients who died in the inpatient unit. The records did not capture support obtained elsewhere, so low uptake may partly reflect support from family, faith communities or primary care."},{"title":"Interventions to increase uptake of bereavement support offered by palliative care services: a systematic review","authors":"Castellanos-Reid M, Obi-Lindgren T, Haddad-Pierce A, Mwangi-Stroud L","year":2023,"venue":"Palliative Care Evidence Reviews","doi":"10.5555/pcer.2023.0152","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We searched four databases to March 2022 for studies of strategies to increase uptake of bereavement support offered by specialist palliative care services. After screening, 14 studies met the inclusion criteria: nine before-after studies, three comparisons between services and two small trials. Proactive personal contact was the strategy most consistently followed by higher uptake. Evidence on timing was mixed, and no included study tested text messages or interpreter-supported outreach. Most studies were at serious risk of bias, and outcome definitions varied from accepting an offer to attending at least one session, which prevented pooling."},{"title":"Text message invitations to bereavement follow-up in a community palliative care service: response by age group","authors":"Rasmussen-Adu K, Villanueva-Grey H","year":2025,"venue":"Community Palliative Care Notes","doi":"10.5555/cpcn.2025.0031","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"A community palliative care service sent a text message invitation to bereavement follow-up to relatives with a mobile number on record, followed by a telephone call to those who did not reply within a week. Of 296 relatives, 41 percent replied to the text message and 29 percent took up support, compared with 22 percent uptake after letters in the previous year. Replies were most frequent among relatives under 60 years of age. Relatives over 75 more often took up support only after the follow-up call. Relatives without a mobile number on record were not invited by text and were analysed separately."},{"title":"Why bereaved relatives decline hospice follow-up: a thematic analysis of free-text feedback forms","authors":"Linwood-Tanaka C, Okafor-Brennan J","year":2020,"venue":"Bereavement Care Practice","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We analysed free-text answers from 263 feedback forms returned by bereaved relatives who had declined an offer of hospice bereavement support. The most common reasons were feeling well supported by family and friends, the offer coming at a time when they were not ready, not knowing what the support involved, and practical barriers such as travel and working hours. Several men wrote that a support group did not suit them and that they would have accepted a one-to-one conversation. Forms were returned by a minority of the relatives who declined, so the reasons may not represent the whole group."}]}
